one_liner: Ahead-of-time WebAssembly-to-C89 translator; the compiled output beat Wasmtime in two independent blog runs.
what_it_does: w2c2 is a command-line translator (also built as a static or shared library, w2c2::w2c2_lib) that turns a .wasm module into C source plus a header; -f N splits the output into files of N functions and -t N translates in parallel. You compile the generated C with w2c2_base.h (and libw2c2wasi for WASI programs) and call the generated <module>Instantiate function and one C function per export. It is not a runtime with a load-module API like Wasmtime: every module is fixed at build time and a changed module means re-translating and recompiling.
how_it_is_fast: Single-pass translation maps each Wasm operand-stack slot to a typed C local and structured control flow to labelled gotos, so the host C compiler (-O3 in examples/coremark) does register allocation, inlining and instruction selection with its full optimizer. Linear-memory loads and stores are memcpy at data+addr, which compile to plain moves. By default (W2C2_RUNTIME_CHECKS=0) every bounds, table and call_indirect type check is compiled out, so part of the gap to Wasmtime is safety work that w2c2 does not do.
when_to_use: Running trusted Wasm (your own C, C++ or Rust built for wasm32-wasi) at near-native speed when you can rebuild per module.
Shipping one Wasm build to many OS and CPU targets, including big-endian PowerPC, SPARC and PA-RISC, classic Mac OS, DOS or old compilers that only accept C89.
CPU-bound workloads where JIT or Cranelift AOT output is 20-40% slower than native (CoreMark, per the Wingo search snippet).
Embedding Wasm-derived code in a C or C++ program with no runtime dependency beyond libc, libm and the optional WASI library.
Translating very large modules with little memory: issue #1 reports clang.wasm (about 25 MB) translated in 5.1 s using 193 MB, versus 1 min 23 s and 1432 MB for wasm2c (2021, hardware not stated).
when_not_to_use: Untrusted modules: the default output has no linear-memory bounds checks and no guard pages (memory comes from calloc/realloc), and no call_indirect index, null or signature checks (issue #76, open since 2023-07-27), so an out-of-bounds Wasm access reads or writes the host heap.
Plugins loaded or hot-swapped at run time: there is no interpreter or JIT, and each module needs a C compiler pass.

Confining a guest's file access: WASI resolvePath returns absolute guest paths unchanged and joins relative paths to the preopen directory without normalizing '..', so a preopen does not restrict which host files a guest can open.
Modules that need proposals the README does not list (SIMD, reference types, exception handling, GC) or memory64 (w2c2_base.h: 'Only support for wasm32 for now').
Threaded modules with the opt-in checks enabled: wasmMemoryCheckRange locks the memory mutex on every load and store to shared memory, a cost no published benchmark measures.

integration.form: source-drop (generated C plus w2c2_base.h); the translator is a CLI, also installable as a static or shared library with a CMake package
integration.dependencies: none for generated code beyond libc and libm; WASI programs link libw2c2wasi; threads need pthreads or Win32 plus the bundled futex library; libdwarf optional for #line mapping; the test suite needs Python 3 and wabt (wast2json, wat2wasm)
integration.min_toolchain: a C89 compiler (README: 'mostly' C89, some common extensions used); CMake 2.8.12+ or Make to build the translator
integration.platforms: any host with a C compiler; README lists x86, ARM, PowerPC, SPARC, PA-RISC (big-endian supported), Mac OS X, Mac OS 9, Haiku, NeXTSTEP, DOS, Windows XP; guest modules wasm32 only
integration.thread_safety: Wasm threads and atomics supported when built with WASM_THREADS_PTHREADS or WASM_THREADS_WIN32; shared memories are preallocated at their maximum size; other thread-safety guarantees not documented
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — replaces running a module under Wasmtime only when the module is known at build time and trusted; the API is generated C functions per export, with no runtime loading and no sandboxing by default

gotchas: W2C2_RUNTIME_CHECKS defaults to 0, which compiles out memory range checks, table bounds, null-element and call_indirect signature checks, atomic alignment traps and data.drop; in that mode addresses are 32-bit, so addr+offset wraps instead of trapping. The opt-in checks arrived on 2026-09-21 (PR #183, no description); the README CoreMark figure and both blog comparisons ran unchecked code.

Harness flaw behind the README's 'passes 99.9% of the core semantics test suite': tests/gen.py emits only single-result assert_return and action commands and silently skips assert_trap, assert_invalid, assert_malformed, assert_exhaustion and multi-result assertions, and the suite builds at -O0. Trap behaviour is covered only by a small dedicated runtime_checks test, so the 99.9% figure says nothing about trapping.
Generated output is large: issue #1 measured 1.3 GiB of C for clang.wasm (versus 301 MiB from wasm2c), so the downstream C compile, not translation, is the build bottleneck; use -f to split files.

A burst of correctness fixes landed on 2026-09-21 (floating-point rounding under GCC optimization, atomic ordering, unsigned division trap reasons, non-recursive control-flow compilation); earlier versions and earlier benchmark runs had those bugs.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick w2c2 over wasm2c (WABT) when you need C89 output for old or big-endian targets or must translate very large modules with little memory; pick wasm2c, or LFI where isolating untrusted code is the goal, and keep WAVM or WasmEdge AOT when modules arrive at run time.
verified_claims_summary: First-party, the README says only 'CoreMark 1.0: ~7% slower than native' (examples/coremark, the wasm3/wasm-coremark module built with -O3; compiler, CPU and native build not stated; no runtime baseline). The faster-than-Wasmtime evidence is independent but read from search snippets only: Frank Denis (2023-12-11, generated C built with zig cc) measured 124.76 s user time under Wasmtime against 73.38 s for w2c2 (1.70x, derived), and Andy Wingo (2025-10-30) found that on CoreMark w2c2 trails native by roughly 4-10% while Wasmtime trails GCC by 30-40%. Hardware is not known for either run, and both ran the default unchecked output.
status_note: Actively maintained (743 commits, last 2026-09-21) and MIT-licensed, so the translator and runtime header are copyable, but treat the default output as native code for trusted modules, not as a sandbox.
sources_read: WebSearch: "w2c2" webassembly benchmark wasmtime "zig cc" "no runtime at all" (snippets of 00f.net posts 2023-12-11 and 2026-07-08)
